claims.text: Anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior in HfNbTaTiZr results from the interplay of temperature-induced microstructural changes and thermal-expansion mismatch.
Temperature-induced microstructural changes in the alloy include dislocation accumulation.
Temperature-induced microstructural changes in the alloy include precipitation.
The alloy contains an intrinsic thermal-expansion mismatch between its matrix and segregated or precipitated regions.
Differential thermal expansion between heterogeneous regions creates internal residual stresses.
The proposed internal residual stresses alter elastic moduli and yield behavior over a wide temperature range.
As-processed HfNbTaTiZr has microstructural heterogeneities relevant to the proposed mechanism.
A minor alloying adjustment can reduce the lattice-parameter difference between phases or segregated regions.
Reducing lattice-parameter differences will reduce thermal-expansion mismatch.
The 600–800 °C regime is associated with precipitation and hardening in HfNbTaTiZr.
High-temperature deformation is governed substantially by dislocation morphology and density.
The alloy undergoes significant microstructural evolution as temperature increases.
Residual stresses generated by microstructural evolution and thermal-expansion mismatch cause non-monotonic yield strength, work hardening, and elastic modulus.
The modified alloy with reduced mismatch will have a more uniform elastic modulus across the tested temperature range than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will show smoother and more predictable yield and hardening behavior than the baseline alloy.
The baseline alloy will show anomalous hardening or softening, potentially including a yield-strength plateau, at 600–800 °C.
The baseline alloy will show mismatch-driven mechanical anomalies near the 1250 °C creep condition.
Mechanical behavior in related high- and medium-entropy alloys depends on temperature and microstructure.
A 20% cold-rolled sample has little rolling-direction dependence in thermal expansion and a microstructure similar to the as-cast sample.
If reducing thermal-expansion mismatch produces no statistically distinguishable reduction in the mechanical and thermoelastic anomalies, the mismatch-driven hypothesis is falsified.
